title: Canadian Economy Surges 3.3 Percent in Q2, Fastest Growth Since 2023
excerpt: Strong export recovery and solid consumer spending propelled Canada's economic rebound, but a new round of US tariffs casts a shadow over the outlook.
body:
• Canada's GDP grew at an annualized rate of 3.3 percent in Q2, the fastest pace since early 2023, after a revised 0.3 percent increase in Q1
  • The upward revision to Q1 means Canada avoided a technical recession after back-to-back quarters of contraction concerns
  • Exports surged 15.1 percent on an annualized quarterly basis, led by passenger cars and light trucks, while consumer spending grew 3.3 percent
  • New 50 percent US tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian exports inject fresh uncertainty into what had been a recovery trajectory

Canada's economy snapped back to life in the second quarter, growing at its fastest pace in more than three years as exports surged, consumers spent more freely, and businesses resumed investing after months of trade-war caution.

Gross domestic product expanded at an annualized rate of 3.3 percent in the April-to-June period, Statistics Canada reported on Friday, a sharp acceleration from a revised 0.3 percent increase in the first quarter. The Q1 revision — which turned what was initially reported as a 0.1 percent contraction into modest growth — means Canada avoided a technical recession.

Exports Lead the Recovery

Net trade provided the biggest boost to growth. Exports jumped 15.1 percent on an annualized quarterly basis, the largest increase in over three years, driven by a rebound in passenger car and light truck shipments following a recovery in auto production, according to TD Economics. Imports rose a muted 1.1 percent by comparison.

Consumer spending grew 3.3 percent at an annualized rate, building on a solid 2.4 percent gain in Q1. Higher spending on financial services, passenger vehicles, and rent drove the gains, while weaker spending on gasoline and food provided an offset.

Business investment swung sharply positive, growing 2.3 percent after contracting 1.3 percent — the first expansion in business fixed capital formation in a year and a half, Al Jazeera reported. Non-residential structures, equipment, and machinery investment rose 12.3 percent on an annualized basis, with investments in computers and data center processing units surging 85 percent, according to TD Economics.

Shadow of New Tariffs

The strong quarter offers Canada a sturdier foundation heading into a fresh round of trade hostilities. President Donald Trump this week imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian exports, and Canada retaliated with its own countermeasures on more than 700 US products.

"It seems like households and businesses were beginning to find ways of navigating the trade-related uncertainty before the latest round of tariffs."

— Royce Mendes, Managing Director, Desjardins

"While it helps that the economy was on stronger footing heading into August, the fresh wave of protectionism injects a significant amount of uncertainty into the outlook," Mendes added.

Michael Davenport, senior Canada economist at Oxford Economics, told Al Jazeera that while GDP growth was along expected lines, "the economy is set to slow in the coming quarters amid escalating US-Canada trade policy uncertainty, new bilateral tariffs, and a shrinking population."

Housing Rebounds, Government Investment Falls

Residential investment jumped 10.4 percent at an annualized rate, nearly reversing the previous quarter's 10.6 percent decline, as resale activity bounced back in Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia alongside stronger apartment construction.

Government consumption spending rose 3.8 percent, but government investment dropped 11.0 percent, continuing a reversal from very strong gains in late 2025, TD Economics noted.

Final domestic demand, the sum of all consumption and capital spending, rebounded to 1 percent in the second quarter from a minor contraction in Q1. Household final consumption expenditure rose 0.8 percent on a quarterly basis, its highest level in three quarters, driven by higher wages and government benefits, according to Statistics Canada data cited by Al Jazeera.

Outlook Uncertain Despite Strong Data

On a monthly basis, GDP rose 0.3 percent in June, above a forecast of 0.2 percent, while an advance indicator showed the economy was largely flat in July. Second-quarter growth of 3.3 percent came in above the Bank of Canada's July forecast of 2.5 percent but slightly below the Reuters consensus estimate of 3.4 percent.

The Canadian dollar weakened slightly after the data, with the loonie trading down 0.01 percent at 72.17 US cents. Money markets were pricing in no change in interest rates at the Bank of Canada's meeting next week.
